1	\section{Discussion}
2	\label{sec:discussion}
3	
4	\paragraph{Why are shape features stationary?}
5	Distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay) remain near-stationary across generation depths, while central-tendency features drift monotonically (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
6	One \emph{speculative} explanation is that shape is primarily determined by the sampling mechanism (temperature, top-$p$ truncation) and the model's architecture-level output distribution, both of which are fixed across generation steps.
7	Recursive generation shifts \emph{what} the model talks about---steering toward higher-probability vocabulary regions---but does not alter \emph{how} the model distributes probability mass around its predictions.
8	If this account is correct, shape features should remain stationary even at much greater depths and across different prompt types, while level features should continue to drift until reaching a fixed point.
9	We flag this as a hypothesis for future investigation, not a conclusion supported by our current experiments.
10	
11	\paragraph{Relation to OOD detection.}
12	Reference-model entropy features are functionally NLL-based out-of-distribution scores---the same signal backbone underlying DetectGPT \cite{detectgpt}, GLTR \cite{gltr}, and Binoculars \cite{binoculars}.
13	Our contribution is not these features per se, but the \emph{ordinal} depth formulation and the empirical finding that they exhibit differential depth response under recursive generation.
14	This connection also offers a lens on shape stationarity: in the OOD detection literature, distributional location statistics (mean log-likelihood) shift under domain drift, while shape statistics (variance, tail behavior) are more robust \cite{ood_baseline}.
15	Recursive generation chains produce an analogous effect---progressive drift away from human text that manifests primarily as a location shift in the NLL distribution.
16	
17	\paragraph{Practical implications.}
18	The differential depth response enables provenance characterization of text corpora.
19	Rather than binary keep-or-discard filtering, practitioners can use depth estimates to understand the composition of their data.
20	Whether this understanding translates to improved curation outcomes remains an open question (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).
21	Three-class granularity separates human text from moderate-drift first-generation content and from deeper text with compounding distributional shift---the distinction most relevant to provenance analysis.
22	Finer-grained depth distinctions may be achievable for non-paraphrastic chains (unlike paraphrastic chains, which converge within $\sim$3 steps \cite{broken_telephone}), but the three-class scheme already captures the practically relevant boundaries.
23	
24	\paragraph{Information value of the negative finding.}
25	Depth-aware curation does not improve downstream language model quality over random subsampling at equal sample count (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Why are shape features stationary?}
Distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay) remain near-stationary across generation depths, while central-tendency features drift monotonically (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
One \emph{speculative} explanation is that shape is primarily determined by the sampling mechanism (temperature, top-$p$ truncation) and the model's architecture-level output distribution, both of which are fixed across generation steps.
Recursive generation shifts \emph{what} the model talks about---steering toward higher-probability vocabulary regions---but does not alter \emph{how} the model distributes probability mass around its predictions.
If this account is correct, shape features should remain stationary even at much greater depths and across different prompt types, while level features should continue to drift until reaching a fixed point.
We flag this as a hypothesis for future investigation, not a conclusion supported by our current experiments.

\paragraph{Relation to OOD detection.}
Reference-model entropy features are functionally NLL-based out-of-distribution scores---the same signal backbone underlying DetectGPT \cite{detectgpt}, GLTR \cite{gltr}, and Binoculars \cite{binoculars}.
Our contribution is not these features per se, but the \emph{ordinal} depth formulation and the empirical finding that they exhibit differential depth response under recursive generation.
This connection also offers a lens on shape stationarity: in the OOD detection literature, distributional location statistics (mean log-likelihood) shift under domain drift, while shape statistics (variance, tail behavior) are more robust \cite{ood_baseline}.
Recursive generation chains produce an analogous effect---progressive drift away from human text that manifests primarily as a location shift in the NLL distribution.

\paragraph{Practical implications.}
The differential depth response enables provenance characterization of text corpora.
Rather than binary keep-or-discard filtering, practitioners can use depth estimates to understand the composition of their data.
Whether this understanding translates to improved curation outcomes remains an open question (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).
Three-class granularity separates human text from moderate-drift first-generation content and from deeper text with compounding distributional shift---the distinction most relevant to provenance analysis.
Finer-grained depth distinctions may be achievable for non-paraphrastic chains (unlike paraphrastic chains, which converge within $\sim$3 steps \cite{broken_telephone}), but the three-class scheme already captures the practically relevant boundaries.

\paragraph{Information value of the negative finding.}
Depth-aware curation does not improve downstream language model quality over random subsampling at equal sample count (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).
This negative result carries positive information value: it rules out depth-based filtering as a data selection strategy, sparing practitioners from building depth-conditional pipelines that would not yield quality gains.
The dominant factor is data quantity, not depth composition---consistent with findings emphasizing data volume over curation sophistication \cite{self_consuming_mad}.

\paragraph{Connection to model collapse.}
Our results relate to, but are distinct from, model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse,self_consuming_mad}.
Model collapse describes distributional degradation when models are \emph{retrained} on their own outputs across generations.
We observe analogous drift---monotonic decrease in vocabulary diversity, compression of perplexity---in \emph{inference chains} without any parameter updates.
This suggests that the mechanisms documented in model collapse theory (regression toward high-probability modes, loss of distributional tails) operate at inference time as well, driven by the sampling process rather than gradient updates.
The shared phenomenology motivates using depth fingerprinting features as early indicators of data that, if fed back into training, may accelerate model collapse.

\paragraph{Topic drift as mediator, not confounder.}

Shape features are near-independent of semantic drift (tail\_decay $|\rho| = 0.068$, $R^2 = 0.005$).
Topic drift is best understood as a \emph{mediator}---one mechanism through which depth manifests---rather than a confound that invalidates depth features.
The depth signal primarily reflects sampling-induced distributional compression, not topic narrowing per se.

drifting features show strong monotonic trends (hapax ratio $\rho = -0.558$, TTR $\rho = -0.542$, entropy mean $\rho = -0.475$),
while shape features show weak or negligible correlations (entropy std $|\rho| = 0.076$, tail decay $|\rho| = 0.089$).

\paragraph{Feature complementarity.}
Table~\ref{tab:ablation} reports ablation results.
The full 7-feature set (F1\,=\,0.789) significantly outperforms both surface-only features (TTR, hapax\_ratio; F1\,=\,0.729) and reference-only features (entropy mean/std/max/min, tail\_decay; F1\,=\,0.745; McNemar $p \approx 0$).
Permutation importance ranks hapax ratio highest (0.269), followed by entropy mean (0.164) and TTR (0.159).
Surface features capture vocabulary impoverishment; reference features capture distributional shift---neither subsumes the other.

\paragraph{Cross-family reference models.}
To confirm that differential depth response is not an artifact of the Pythia-410M reference model, we compute features using three cross-family references: Pythia-410M, OLMo-2-1B, and Qwen3-0.6B.
All three achieve LOGO F1 between 0.80 and 0.82, with consistent drift directions across features.
The pattern generalizes across reference model architectures.

\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Feature set} & \textbf{LOGO F1} & \textbf{Top feature (importance)} \\
\midrule
Full (7 features)     & 0.789 & hapax\_ratio (0.269) \\
Surface only (2)      & 0.729 & hapax\_ratio (0.320) \\
Reference only (5)    & 0.745 & entropy\_mean (0.218) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Feature ablation (6-gen LOGO). Full $>$ surface = reference confirms complementarity between surface diversity features and reference-model distributional features.}
\label{tab:ablation}
\end{table}

Leave-one-feature-out analysis confirms that 6 of 7 features contribute positively, with entropy\_max showing the largest marginal impact despite modest split frequency (Appendix~\ref{app:lofo}).


\subsection{Comparison with Detection Baselines}
\label{sec:results-baselines}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig3_baseline_comparison.png}
\caption{LOGO macro-F1 with 95\% bootstrap confidence intervals for each detection baseline and the 7-feature ensemble. Per-generator held-out F1 varies more for single detectors than for the ensemble.}
\label{fig:baseline-ci}
\end{figure}

We repurpose four existing detection scores as ordinal depth predictors by training the same ordinal classifier on each score as a single feature, using identical LOGO evaluation (Figure~\ref{fig:baseline-ci}).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Method} & \textbf{LOGO F1} & \textbf{95\% CI} \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{3}{l}{\textit{Multi-detector ensembles}} \\
4-det.\ + surface (6 feat.) & \textbf{0.805} & [0.800, 0.809] \\
4-detector ens.\ (4 feat.)  & 0.796 & [0.792, 0.801] \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{3}{l}{\textit{Single-model methods}} \\
7-feature ensemble    & \textbf{0.789} & [0.783, 0.792] \\
Avg-LogProb           & 0.737 & [0.732, 0.742] \\
FastDetectGPT         & 0.688 & [0.683, 0.693] \\
LD-Score              & 0.655 & [0.649, 0.660] \\
Binoculars            & 0.416 & [0.411, 0.422] \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Ordinal depth classification: all methods under unified 6-gen LOGO evaluation. The 7-feature ensemble outperforms all individual detection baselines; multi-detector ensembles achieve higher accuracy at the cost of running multiple detection pipelines.}
\label{tab:baselines}
\end{table}
The 7-feature ensemble outperforms every individual detection baseline: +5.2\,pp over Avg-LogProb ($p < 0.001$), +10.1\,pp over FastDetectGPT, +13.4\,pp over LD-Score, and +37.3\,pp over Binoculars (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}).

The critical distinction is \emph{reliability}.
The ensemble achieves per-generator F1 ranging from 0.683 to 0.856 (std\,=\,0.058).
While this range reflects genuine difficulty variation across generators---particularly at larger scales (\S\ref{sec:results-classification})---the ensemble provides reliable performance even for the most challenging generator (Qwen3-8B: 0.683).
Each single detector captures partial depth signal---Avg-LogProb tracks mean perplexity shift, LD-Score captures character-level distributional change---but each fails on specific generator families.
The 7-feature ensemble aggregates complementary signals, producing stable performance regardless of the held-out generator.
The overall 95\% bootstrap CI [0.783, 0.792] reflects sampling precision of the pooled estimate, not cross-generator consistency.

\paragraph{Multi-detector ensembles.}
The multi-detector ensembles (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}) confirm that combining detection scores yields stronger depth signal.
Adding our surface features (TTR, hapax ratio) to the 4-detector ensemble further improves performance, confirming that surface diversity features capture signal complementary to detection scores.
However, multi-detector approaches require running multiple detection pipelines, while the 7-feature method uses a single lightweight reference model plus two vocabulary statistics.
The practical advantage of depth features lies in their interpretability---they reveal the differential depth response pattern (\S\ref{sec:results-differential})---and computational efficiency.
Baseline results are stable across classifier hyperparameters: using the ensemble's settings ($n\_\text{estimators}{=}200$, $\max\_\text{depth}{=}6$) instead of the default ($100$/$3$) changes baseline F1 by less than 0.002\,pp for all four detectors, confirming that performance differences reflect feature informativeness rather than classifier capacity.

\paragraph{Gen-0 data leakage control.}
Because gen-0 (human-written) seed texts are shared across all generators, LOGO evaluation creates a train--test overlap for the gen-0 class.
To verify that depth discrimination is not driven by this overlap, we evaluate all methods on a binary task (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) excluding gen-0 entirely (Table~\ref{tab:binary-logo}).
The 7-feature ensemble achieves binary LOGO F1\,=\,0.723, well above chance and consistent with the 3-class gen-1 and gen-2+ per-class F1 scores (0.64 and 0.80 respectively; \S\ref{sec:results-classification}).
The depth signal between gen-1 and gen-2+ is genuine and does not depend on the gen-0 overlap.

\toprule
\textbf{Method} & \textbf{Binary F1} & \textbf{95\% CI} \\
\midrule

4-detector ens.\     & 0.712 & [0.705, 0.718] \\
LD-Score             & 0.701 & [0.694, 0.707] \\
FastDetectGPT        & 0.616 & [0.609, 0.622] \\
Binoculars           & 0.524 & [0.517, 0.531] \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Binary depth classification (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+, gen-0 excluded) under 6-gen LOGO. Excluding gen-0 removes the shared-seed data overlap; depth discrimination remains significant.}
\label{tab:binary-logo}
\end{table}


\subsection{Downstream Utility: A Negative Finding}
\label{sec:results-downstream}

Can depth-aware data curation improve downstream language model quality?
We fine-tune OLMo-2-0425-1B on five data variants (3 seeds each) and evaluate perplexity on a held-out test set (Table~\ref{tab:downstream}).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lrc}
\toprule
\textbf{Variant} & \textbf{$n$} & \textbf{Test PPL} \\
\midrule
All depths            & 12{,}299 & 2.335 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Size-matched (random) & 3{,}951  & 2.367 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Depth 0--1 only       & 3{,}951  & 2.387 $\pm$ 0.001 \\
Binary-filtered       & 3{,}951  & 2.389 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Depth 0 only          & 797      & 2.681 $\pm$ 0.001 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Downstream fine-tuning perplexity (OLMo-2-0425-1B, mean $\pm$ std across 3 seeds). At equal sample count, random subsampling (2.367) outperforms depth-aware curation (depth 0--1: 2.387, binary-filtered: 2.389).}
\label{tab:downstream}
\end{table}

The results are unambiguous: data quantity dominates depth composition.
Training on all 12{,}299 samples yields the lowest perplexity (2.335).
At equal sample count ($n$\,=\,3{,}951), random subsampling (2.367) \emph{outperforms} both depth-stratified selection (depth 0--1: 2.387) and binary detection filtering (2.389).
Cross-seed variance is below 0.002 across all variants, confirming the robustness of this null result.

Restricting training to human-only text (depth 0, $n$\,=\,797) produces a sharp perplexity increase to 2.681, driven primarily by the 5$\times$ reduction in data volume rather than depth composition per se.

We report this negative finding transparently: depth fingerprinting is an effective \emph{diagnostic} tool for characterizing text provenance, not a \emph{curative} tool for data curation.
Knowing the generation depth of a document does not, by itself, make it more or less useful for training.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Web-crawled corpora are the dominant source of pretraining data for large language models (LLMs), yet an increasing fraction of this data is itself LLM-generated.
Estimates suggest that 7--17\% of recent scientific papers and peer reviews contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}, and this proportion continues to grow as generated text enters the web and becomes seed material for subsequent generation.
The result is recursive generation chains whose outputs progressively diverge from human-written text---a problem that current detection methods are ill-equipped to address.

Existing detectors \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt} provide binary real-vs-synthetic classification, forcing an all-or-nothing filtering decision: discard everything flagged as synthetic, losing potentially useful first-generation content, or retain everything, admitting text with compounding distributional drift.
This conflates qualitatively different material.
A first-generation continuation---an LLM expanding a human-written passage---retains much of the source distribution's lexical and structural properties.
A third- or fourth-generation text, conditioned recursively on prior LLM outputs, exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity, compressed perplexity, and narrower token probability distributions.
Treating these as a single ``synthetic'' category discards provenance information that could inform risk-stratified curation decisions.

We argue that a finer-grained characterization is needed: \emph{ordinal depth estimation}, the task of classifying text into generation depth classes (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than producing a binary label.
We refer to the overall framework---features, classifier, and evaluation protocol---as \emph{depth fingerprinting}, distinguishing the method from the task it addresses.
No existing method addresses this task directly in non-paraphrastic continuation chains.
When repurposed as ordinal depth predictors, individual detection scores exhibit high cross-generator variance---confidence intervals spanning 0.41--0.82 in macro-F1 (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines})---making any single detector unreliable across unknown generators.
Concurrent work on iterative paraphrasing chains \cite{broken_telephone,markovian_chains} analyzes convergence behavior under semantic-preservation constraints, which bound distinguishable depth classes to approximately three.
These results do not extend to \emph{non-paraphrastic} generation chains (e.g., continuation), where the absence of semantic anchoring permits richer depth signal.
We focus on non-paraphrastic continuation chains from base (pretrained) models; instruction-tuned and RLHF models, which dominate web text, remain untested (Limitations).

We study distributional drift in non-paraphrastic LLM generation chains across six generators from three model families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen; 0.6B--8.2B parameters).
We characterize a \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity features---including reference-model mean entropy (functionally an NLL-based out-of-distribution score \cite{ood_baseline}), type-token ratio, and hapax ratio---drift monotonically with generation depth, while distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay) remain near-stationary.
This pattern is consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the NLL distribution: text becomes progressively more predictable on average while the functional form of the distribution is preserved.
The combination of drifting and stationary features yields a 7-feature ensemble that achieves leave-one-generator-out (LOGO) macro-F1 of 0.79, with per-generator held-out F1 ranging from 0.68 to 0.86.
The practical advantage is reliability across unknown generators.

We also report a negative finding.
Depth-aware data curation---selecting training data based on estimated generation depth---does not improve downstream language model quality compared to random subsampling at equal sample count (perplexity: 2.367 random vs.\ 2.387 depth-stratified).
In our experimental setting, depth fingerprinting is an effective \emph{diagnostic} tool for characterizing text provenance, not a \emph{curative} tool for data selection.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item \textbf{Task formulation.} We define ordinal generation depth estimation as a task beyond binary detection, providing a framework for finer-grained provenance characterization of web-crawled text.
    \item \textbf{Empirical characterization.} We characterize differential depth response across six generators spanning three model families (0.6B--8.2B): a 7-feature ensemble combining drifting and stationary features achieves LOGO F1\,=\,0.79, outperforming all individual detection baselines ($p < 0.001$), with per-generator held-out F1 ranging from 0.68 to 0.86.
    \item \textbf{Complementary analysis.} As a complementary analysis, we show that depth-aware data curation does not improve downstream language model quality compared to random subsampling, establishing depth fingerprinting as a diagnostic rather than curative tool.
\end{enumerate}

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
\S\ref{sec:related} surveys related work on text detection, model collapse, and data quality.
\S\ref{sec:method} describes generation chain construction, feature extraction, and evaluation protocol.
\S\ref{sec:results} presents classification results, differential depth response analysis, baseline comparisons, and the downstream utility experiment.
\S\ref{sec:discussion} discusses implications, and a separate Limitations section addresses scope boundaries.

14	This connection also offers a lens on shape stationarity: in the OOD detection literature, distributional location statistics (mean log-likelihood) shift under domain drift, while shape statistics (variance, tail behavior) are more robust \cite{ood_baseline}.
15	Recursive generation chains produce an analogous effect---progressive drift away from human text that manifests primarily as a location shift in the NLL distribution.
16	
17	\paragraph{Practical implications.}
18	The differential depth response enables provenance characterization of text corpora.
19	Rather than binary keep-or-discard filtering, practitioners can use depth estimates to understand the composition of their data.
20	Whether this understanding translates to improved curation outcomes remains an open question (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).

22	Finer-grained depth distinctions may be achievable for non-paraphrastic chains (unlike paraphrastic chains, which converge within $\sim$3 steps \cite{broken_telephone}), but the three-class scheme already captures the practically relevant boundaries.
23

25	Depth-aware curation does not improve downstream language model quality over random subsampling at equal sample count (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).
26	This negative result carries positive information value: it rules out depth-based filtering as a data selection strategy, sparing practitioners from building depth-conditional pipelines that would not yield quality gains.

A first-generation continuation---an LLM expanding a human-written passage---retains much of the source distribution's lexical and structural properties.
A third- or fourth-generation text, conditioned recursively on prior LLM outputs, exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity, compressed perplexity, and narrower token probability distributions.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Why are shape features stationary?}
Distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay) remain near-stationary across generation depths, while central-tendency features drift monotonically (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
One \emph{speculative} explanation is that shape is primarily determined by the sampling mechanism (temperature, top-$p$ truncation) and the model's architecture-level output distribution, both of which are fixed across generation steps.
Recursive generation shifts \emph{what} the model talks about---steering toward higher-probability vocabulary regions---but does not alter \emph{how} the model distributes probability mass around its predictions.
If this account is correct, shape features should remain stationary even at much greater depths and across different prompt types, while level features should continue to drift until reaching a fixed point.
We flag this as a hypothesis for future investigation, not a conclusion supported by our current experiments.

\paragraph{Relation to OOD detection.}
Reference-model entropy features are functionally NLL-based out-of-distribution scores---the same signal backbone underlying DetectGPT \cite{detectgpt}, GLTR \cite{gltr}, and Binoculars \cite{binoculars}.
Our contribution is not these features per se, but the \emph{ordinal} depth formulation and the empirical finding that they exhibit differential depth response under recursive generation.
This connection also offers a lens on shape stationarity: in the OOD detection literature, distributional location statistics (mean log-likelihood) shift under domain drift, while shape statistics (variance, tail behavior) are more robust \cite{ood_baseline}.
Recursive generation chains produce an analogous effect---progressive drift away from human text that manifests primarily as a location shift in the NLL distribution.

\paragraph{Practical implications.}
The differential depth response enables provenance characterization of text corpora.
Rather than binary keep-or-discard filtering, practitioners can use depth estimates to understand the composition of their data.
Whether this understanding translates to improved curation outcomes remains an open question (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).
Three-class granularity separates human text from moderate-drift first-generation content and from deeper text with compounding distributional shift---the distinction most relevant to provenance analysis.
Finer-grained depth distinctions may be achievable for non-paraphrastic chains (unlike paraphrastic chains, which converge within $\sim$3 steps \cite{broken_telephone}), but the three-class scheme already captures the practically relevant boundaries.

\paragraph{Information value of the negative finding.}
Depth-aware curation does not improve downstream language model quality over random subsampling at equal sample count (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).
This negative result carries positive information value: it rules out depth-based filtering as a data selection strategy, sparing practitioners from building depth-conditional pipelines that would not yield quality gains.
The dominant factor is data quantity, not depth composition---consistent with findings emphasizing data volume over curation sophistication \cite{self_consuming_mad}.

\paragraph{Connection to model collapse.}
Our results relate to, but are distinct from, model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse,self_consuming_mad}.
Model collapse describes distributional degradation when models are \emph{retrained} on their own outputs across generations.
We observe analogous drift---monotonic decrease in vocabulary diversity, compression of perplexity---in \emph{inference chains} without any parameter updates.
This suggests that the mechanisms documented in model collapse theory (regression toward high-probability modes, loss of distributional tails) operate at inference time as well, driven by the sampling process rather than gradient updates.
The shared phenomenology motivates using depth fingerprinting features as early indicators of data that, if fed back into training, may accelerate model collapse.

\paragraph{Topic drift as mediator, not confounder.}
Recursive generation narrows topic diversity: cosine similarity between adjacent depths increases monotonically from 0.62 (depth 0$\to$1) to 0.86 (depth 3$\to$4), consistent with regression toward high-probability modes.
However, topic narrowing accounts for less than 9\% of feature variance (maximum: entropy\_mean, $\rho = -0.286$, $R^2 = 0.082$).
Shape features are near-independent of semantic drift (tail\_decay $|\rho| = 0.068$, $R^2 = 0.005$).
Topic drift is best understood as a \emph{mediator}---one mechanism through which depth manifests---rather than a confound that invalidates depth features.
The depth signal primarily reflects sampling-induced distributional compression, not topic narrowing per se.

\paragraph{Depth features vs.\ multi-detector ensembles.}
In 3-class evaluation, multi-detector ensembles achieve marginally higher F1 (0.805 with surface features added vs.\ 0.789).
However, this advantage is driven entirely by gen-0 classification, where detection scores excel at human-vs-machine discrimination.
In the leak-free binary evaluation (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+), the 7-feature ensemble matches the best multi-detector configuration (0.723 vs.\ 0.724), demonstrating that depth features capture the gen-1/gen-2+ distinction as effectively as four detection pipelines combined.
Depth features additionally offer interpretability---they reveal the differential depth response pattern---and computational efficiency, requiring only a single lightweight reference model.

\paragraph{Same-family reference bias.}
Pythia-1B achieves the highest held-out F1 (0.856) despite using a same-family reference model (Pythia-410M).
Cross-family references (OLMo-2-1B, Qwen3-0.6B) yield nearly identical Pythia-1B F1 (0.845--0.848), confirming that this generator's high detectability reflects its intrinsic generation patterns rather than reference-model family bias.

102	\subsection{Comparison with Detection Baselines}
103	\label{sec:results-baselines}
104	
105	\begin{figure}[t]
106	\centering
107	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig3_baseline_comparison.png}

109	\label{fig:baseline-ci}
110	\end{figure}
111	
112	We repurpose four existing detection scores as ordinal depth predictors by training the same classifier on each score as a single feature, using identical LOGO evaluation.
113	Because gen-0 seed texts are shared across generators (\S\ref{sec:generation}), 3-class LOGO evaluation creates a train--test overlap for the gen-0 class.
114	We therefore report both 3-class and binary (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) results; the binary metric is the primary measure of depth discrimination (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}).
115	
116	\begin{table}[t]
117	\centering
118	\small
119	\begin{tabular}{lccc}
120	\toprule
121	\textbf{Method} & \textbf{3-class F1} & \textbf{Binary F1} & \textbf{Per-gen std} \\
122	\midrule
123	7-feature ensemble    & 0.789 & \textbf{0.723} & 0.051 \\
124	4-det.\ + surface     & \textbf{0.805} & 0.724 & 0.049 \\
125	4-detector ens.\      & 0.796 & 0.712 & 0.044 \\
126	Avg-LogProb           & 0.737 & 0.712 & 0.044 \\
127	LD-Score              & 0.655 & 0.701 & 0.045 \\
128	FastDetectGPT         & 0.688 & 0.616 & 0.056 \\
129	Binoculars            & 0.417 & 0.524 & 0.022 \\
130	\bottomrule
131	\end{tabular}
132	\caption{Depth classification under unified 6-gen LOGO evaluation. \textbf{3-class}: gen-0/gen-1/gen-2+ (gen-0 samples shared across generators; see \S\ref{sec:generation}). \textbf{Binary}: gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ only, eliminating the gen-0 train--test overlap. Per-gen std measures cross-generator consistency of the binary metric. The 7-feature ensemble is the strongest single-model method on both metrics and matches the best multi-detector ensemble on binary F1.}
133	\label{tab:baselines}
134	\end{table}
135	
136	The 7-feature ensemble achieves binary F1\,=\,0.723, outperforming every individual detection baseline: +1.1\,pp over Avg-LogProb, +2.2\,pp over LD-Score, +10.7\,pp over FastDetectGPT, and +19.9\,pp over Binoculars ($p < 0.001$ for all comparisons).
137	On the 3-class metric, the ensemble (0.789) similarly outperforms all single baselines, though the margins are inflated by the gen-0 overlap.
138	
139	\paragraph{Multi-detector ensembles.}
140	Combining all four detection scores into a 4-detector ensemble yields binary F1\,=\,0.712---below the 7-feature ensemble (0.723).
141	The multi-detector advantage seen in 3-class evaluation (0.796 vs.\ 0.789) is driven entirely by superior gen-0 classification; existing detectors excel at human-vs-machine discrimination but do not capture the finer depth signal between gen-1 and gen-2+.
142	Adding our surface features (TTR, hapax ratio) to the 4-detector ensemble raises binary F1 to 0.724, matching the 7-feature ensemble and confirming that surface diversity features capture signal complementary to detection scores.
143	Baseline results are stable across classifier hyperparameters: using the ensemble's settings ($n\_\text{estimators}{=}200$, $\max\_\text{depth}{=}6$) instead of the default ($100$/$3$) changes baseline F1 by less than 0.002\,pp, confirming that performance differences reflect feature informativeness rather than classifier capacity.
144	
145	\paragraph{Binoculars: a non-transferable signal.}
146	Binoculars achieves near-random performance on the depth task (3-class F1\,=\,0.417, binary F1\,=\,0.524), confirming that cross-model perplexity ratios---the core signal in Binoculars---do not transfer to depth discrimination.

152	Can depth-aware data curation improve downstream language model quality?
153	We fine-tune OLMo-2-0425-1B on five data variants (3 seeds each) and evaluate perplexity on a held-out test set (Table~\ref{tab:downstream}).
154

156	\centering
157	\small
158	\begin{tabular}{lrc}
159	\toprule
160	\textbf{Variant} & \textbf{$n$} & \textbf{Test PPL} \\
161	\midrule
162	All depths            & 12{,}299 & 2.335 $\pm$ 0.000 \\

164	Depth 0--1 only       & 3{,}951  & 2.387 $\pm$ 0.001 \\

167	\bottomrule
168	\end{tabular}
169	\caption{Downstream fine-tuning perplexity (OLMo-2-0425-1B, mean $\pm$ std across 3 seeds). At equal sample count, random subsampling (2.367) outperforms depth-aware curation (depth 0--1: 2.387, binary-filtered: 2.389).}
170	\label{tab:downstream}
171	\end{table}
172	
173	The results are unambiguous: data quantity dominates depth composition.
174	Training on all 12{,}299 samples yields the lowest perplexity (2.335).
175	At equal sample count ($n$\,=\,3{,}951), random subsampling (2.367) \emph{outperforms} both depth-stratified selection (depth 0--1: 2.387) and binary detection filtering (2.389).
176	Cross-seed variance is below 0.002 across all variants, confirming the robustness of this null result.
177	
178	Restricting training to human-only text (depth 0, $n$\,=\,797) produces a sharp perplexity increase to 2.681, driven primarily by the 5$\times$ reduction in data volume rather than depth composition per se.
